questions.prompt: An investor buys a callable corporate bond. Which pair of positions does the investor hold?
choices: Long a straight bond and long a call option on it
Long a straight bond and short a call option on it
Short a straight bond and long a call option on it
Long a straight bond and long a put option on it
questions.explanation: The issuer holds the right to buy the bond back at the call price, so the investor has written (is short) that call. Callable price = straight price − call option value.

questions.prompt: A bond pays a 7% annual coupon, has 8 years to maturity, and is callable from year 2 at 103 (per 100 of face value). It trades at 105, where its yield to maturity is 6.19%. What is its yield to worst? Answer in percent, to two decimals.
questions.explanation: Start with the first call date: solve 105 = 7/(1+y) + (7 + 103)/(1+y)². With x = 1 + y this is 105x² − 7x − 110 = 0, so x = 1.0574 and the yield to first call is 5.74%. That is below the 6.19% yield to maturity, and later call dates give more (6.07% for a call in year 3), so the yield to worst is 5.74%.

questions.prompt: A bond is already callable, and market yields fall well below its coupon rate. Which statements are true?
choices: Its price stays close to the call price
It is worth more than an otherwise identical bond that cannot be called
A further fall in yields raises its price far less than it raises a straight bond's price
The issuer is likely to call the bond and borrow again at the lower rate
questions.explanation: A call is now likely, so the price cannot rise much above the call price while a straight bond's price keeps climbing. That flattening is negative convexity. A callable bond is never worth more than the same bond without the call: the investor is short the option.

questions.prompt: A bond pays a 6% annual coupon and will first be callable in 2 years at 102 (per 100 of face value). The market yield is 3%, low enough that a call in 2 years is certain. What is the bond worth today, per 100 of face value?
questions.explanation: With a certain call the bond is worth its price to call: 6/1.03 + (6 + 102)/1.03² = 5.83 + 101.80 = 107.63. It is above 102 because two above-market coupons are still safe during call protection.

questions.prompt: A bond has a make-whole call at the Treasury yield plus 0.25%, and investors price the bond at the Treasury yield plus 1%. Treasury yields fall sharply. Why is calling the bond not a cheap way to refinance?
choices: A make-whole call may be used only in the final year before maturity, when little interest is left to save
The make-whole price is fixed on the day the bond is issued, and that fixed price is far above face value
The make-whole price discounts the remaining payments at a rate below the bond's market yield, so it stays above the market value
The investor, not the issuer, decides whether the call is used, and will refuse once yields have fallen
questions.explanation: The issuer must pay the remaining payments discounted at Treasury + 0.25%, a lower rate than the Treasury + 1% the market uses. That price is above the bond's market value and climbs as Treasury yields fall, so there is no cheap refinancing and no price ceiling.
